title: Trust Calibration — Neither Overtrust Nor Undertrust
content:
Calibrated trust is the difference between an AI that augments judgement and one that displaces it. Overtrust causes harm when the system is wrong. Undertrust wastes it when it is right. Neither shows up in accuracy metrics.

WHAT SHAPES TRUST IN THE MOMENT, whether you design for it or not:
- SURFACE CONFIDENCE — how certain the output sounds, independent of whether it should.
- TRACK RECORD — prior interactions, this session and previous ones.
- STAKES LEGIBILITY — how clearly the user understands what could go wrong.
- SOURCE VISIBILITY — whether reasoning, sources, or alternatives are shown.
- PERSONA FIT — a 'professional' persona is trusted more than a 'friendly' one for identical content.

THE FIVE TRUST FAILURE MODES:
- SYCOPHANCY OVERTRUST — the system agrees with the user, who trusts the agreement and acts on it. The worst failure, because it compounds across turns.
- CONFIDENCE-MISMATCH OVERTRUST — certainty about something it should not be certain about.
- DEFENSIVE UNDERTRUST — hedging everything, so the user tunes out the qualifier, including the important one.
- AUTHORITY COLLAPSE — one wrong answer in a high-stakes context destroys trust in the whole product.
- TRUST LAUNDERING — low-confidence content in high-confidence formatting. Bold headers and decisive bullets give visual authority to epistemic uncertainty.

DECISION RULES:
- High stakes + low confidence → bias toward undertrust. The cost of acting on bad information exceeds the cost of an extra verification step.
- If the user has corrected the system this session, raise hedging on similar outputs for the rest of it — and show the update.
- Never inflate confidence to match the user's apparent expectation.
- Prefer 'I don't know' to a confident wrong answer. Its trust cost is lower than being caught wrong.
- If the system changes position under pushback, name the update. Silent flips destroy trust faster than disagreement.
source: Owl-Listener/ai-design-skills (MIT), adapted and extended; Lee & See (2004) on appropriate reliance

title: The Trust Calibration Matrix — Language by Stakes and Confidence
content:
A working rubric for how confidently the system should speak.

| Stakes | Confidence | Language |
|---|---|---|
| Low | Low | 'Best guess: X. Easy to check by Y.' |
| Low | High | Direct answer, no hedge. |
| Medium | Low | 'I'd suggest X based on Y. If your situation differs, check with Z.' |
| Medium | High | Direct answer plus a one-line source. |
| High | Low | 'I'm not the right tool for this. Try Z.' |
| High | High | Direct answer, source, and a recommended verification step. |

WORKED EXAMPLE — a user asks an assistant 'is it safe to take ibuprofen with my blood thinner?' Stakes: high. Confidence: low, because the system has no patient record. Correct response: decline the specific advice, explain that the answer depends on which anticoagulant and the dosage, and route to a prescriber or pharmacist with a note that many offer free phone consults. Note what this does — it declines without being useless.

THE CONFIDENCE-LANGUAGE RUBRIC to build alongside it:
- BANNED PHRASES: 'I'm 100% sure', and 'always' or 'never' without justification.
- APPROVED PHRASES tied to actual confidence levels: 'I'm fairly sure', 'I'd verify this', 'I don't know'. Used because they are true, not as decoration.

ANTI-PATTERNS TO AUDIT FOR:
- UNIVERSAL HEDGING — every output ending with 'but you should verify'. The qualifier loses all signal and reads as legal cover.
- CONFIDENCE THEATRE — decisive formatting applied to uncertain content.
- APOLOGY AS TRUST-BUILDING — over-apologising signals incompetence. One clean acknowledgement is more trustworthy than five.
- PERSONA-DRIVEN CONFIDENCE — the persona dictating certainty rather than the epistemic state.
- TRUST TRANSFER BY ASSOCIATION — 'powered by [model]' framed as a correctness guarantee. Pedigree is not accuracy in a specific case.

title: Transparency Patterns — Showing the Work
content:
Transparency is the mechanism; calibrated trust is the outcome. These are the patterns that deliver it.

WHAT TO SHOW:
- SOURCES, inline and clickable, at the specific claim rather than as a bibliography. A citation the user can check in one click is worth more than a paragraph about reliability.
- RETRIEVED CONTEXT — which documents, which passages, which records informed this answer.
- TOOL USE, as it happens. 'Searched inventory', 'Read Q3-report.pdf', 'Ran the query'. This is the single most effective transparency pattern in agentic products, because it is legible progress and evidence simultaneously.
- REASONING, summarised and collapsible. Full chain-of-thought is usually noise; a three-line summary of the approach is signal.
- ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED — 'two readings of this: A and B; I went with A because…'. Shows the working and gives the user a specific thing to redirect.
- WHAT IT DID NOT DO. In agentic contexts, the actions considered and skipped matter as much as the actions taken.

WHAT NOT TO SHOW:
- Raw model internals, token probabilities, or embedding scores. Precision the user cannot act on is noise dressed as honesty.
- A numeric confidence percentage. Users systematically misread these, and they imply a calibration most systems do not have. Prefer language bands.
- Every reasoning step by default. Make it available, not mandatory.

DESIGN MECHANICS:
- Progressive: a claim, then a source marker, then the passage, then the full document. Three levels, each one click.
- Attribution should survive copy-paste. Output that loses its citations when moved becomes an unsourced assertion in someone else's document.
- Make the absence of a source explicit. 'I don't have a source for this' is a transparency pattern, and it is the one most often omitted.

THE HARD TRADE-OFF: transparency costs interface and attention. Resolve it by tying disclosure depth to stakes — a casual answer needs a source marker; a financial or medical one needs the passage visible without a click.

title: Guardrail and Refusal Design
content:
Guardrails are the constraints on system behaviour. Their design is a UX problem, not only a policy one, because a badly designed refusal does more damage than the behaviour it prevented.

THE FOUR THINGS A USER MIGHT HIT, which must be distinguishable:
1. CANNOT — a capability limit. 'I can't access your calendar.'
2. WILL NOT — a policy boundary. 'I won't help with that.'
3. NOT ENOUGH INFORMATION — an input problem. 'I need to know which account.'
4. SOMETHING BROKE — a system failure. 'The service is unavailable.'
Collapsing these into one message destroys the user's ability to adapt. This is the most common refusal-design failure.

WHAT A GOOD REFUSAL CONTAINS:
- The boundary, stated plainly and in one sentence. No lecture.
- Whether it is a capability or a policy limit, so the user knows whether to rephrase or to stop.
- The nearest thing the system CAN do. A refusal with an adjacent offer is helpful; a bare refusal is a wall.
- No moralising and no repetition. Saying it once is respectful; saying it three ways is a reprimand.

FENCE-POSTING — stating the boundary BEFORE the user hits it. 'I can help with X but not Y' at the top of an interaction prevents the failed attempt entirely, and it is the cheapest guardrail design available.

GRACEFUL DEGRADATION: when the system cannot fully help, partial help beats total failure. If it can do three of four steps, do three and name the fourth. Products that fail all-or-nothing feel far more limited than they are.

ANTI-PATTERNS:
- The refusal that does not say why.
- The refusal that lectures.
- Inconsistent boundaries — refusing something it did last week, or refusing one phrasing and accepting another. Inconsistency reads as arbitrary and destroys the user's model of the system.
- A refusal with no path forward.

title: Consent and Agency — Keeping the Human in Charge
content:
Agency is preserved by design decisions, and eroded by defaults.

THE AGENCY CHECKLIST for any AI feature:
- CAN THE USER STOP IT? A visible, always-available stop on any generation or action. Non-negotiable.
- CAN THE USER UNDO IT? For any action with an external effect — a sent message, a changed record, a committed file — undo or an approval gate.
- IS THE DEFAULT OPT-IN OR OPT-OUT? Anything that uses the user's content for training, personalisation, or memory should be opt-in, visibly.
- DOES THE USER KNOW WHAT IT WILL DO BEFORE IT DOES IT? Preview before commit for anything consequential. 'I'm about to send this to these twelve people' — shown, not summarised.
- CAN THE USER OVERRIDE IT? A suggestion the user cannot reject is a decision, not a suggestion.
- CAN THE USER SEE WHAT IT KNOWS? Inspectable, editable, deletable memory.

CONSENT SURFACES THAT ARE OFTEN MISSED:
- Content leaving the device or going to a third-party model.
- Implicit personalisation from behaviour rather than from stated preference.
- The system acting on the user's behalf with their identity — sending, posting, committing, paying.
- Retention. How long is this kept, and can the user end it?

WHERE AGENCY TIPS INTO MANIPULATION: when the system's persuasive capability is used to steer rather than to inform. A system that argues back when the user declines a suggestion, that re-offers what was rejected, or that frames the user's choice as a mistake has crossed from assistance into pressure. The line is whether the user's stated preference survives.

THE TEST: could the user explain, accurately, what the system will do with their input and on their behalf? If not, you do not have consent — you have a dialog they clicked through.

title: Harm Anticipation — Finding the Failure Modes Before Launch
content:
A structured pass over how the feature hurts someone. Do it before launch, in writing, with the team.

THE DIMENSIONS TO WALK:
- WRONG-ANSWER HARM. What happens if a user acts on incorrect output? Trace it to a real consequence: money lost, a wrong dose, a missed deadline, a broken build, a bad hire.
- CONFIDENT-WRONG HARM. The same, but where the output was persuasive. Higher likelihood of being acted on.
- OMISSION HARM. What happens if the system leaves something out? A summary that drops the caveat, a search that misses the relevant record.
- MISUSE. How would someone use this deliberately to harm another person? Harassment, impersonation, fraud, generating plausible misinformation at volume.
- DISPARATE IMPACT. Which users does it work worse for? Non-native speakers, users with unusual data, users in under-represented contexts, users with assistive technology.
- DEPENDENCE HARM. What atrophies if users rely on this? Skill loss is a real cost in professional tools and it is rarely counted.
- PRIVACY HARM. What gets exposed, to whom, and by what path — including through the output itself.
- SCALE HARM. What is fine once and harmful ten thousand times?

THE METHOD:
1. For each dimension, write the specific scenario. Named user, real action, concrete consequence. Generic risks produce generic mitigations.
2. Rate likelihood and severity.
3. For the top items, decide: prevent (design it out), mitigate (reduce the damage), detect (notice it happening), or accept (and say so explicitly).
4. Write the detection signal for anything you accepted. An accepted risk with no monitoring is an unmanaged risk.

WHY DESIGN OWNS THIS: most mitigations are interface decisions — a confirmation, a preview, a hedge, a source, a rate limit, a refusal, a disclosure. Policy sets the boundary; design determines whether the user encounters it usefully.

title: Escalation Design — Knowing When to Hand Off
content:
Knowing when NOT to handle something is a trust-building behaviour, not a failure. Designing the handoff badly wastes it.

WHEN TO ESCALATE:
- Stakes exceed the system's confidence (see at-002).
- The domain is regulated — medical, legal, financial advice.
- The user is distressed, and the correct response is a human, not a better answer.
- The task requires authority the system does not have — an exception, a refund beyond a threshold, a policy override.
- Repeated failure. After two failed repair attempts, escalate rather than trying a third time.
- The user asks for a human. Always honour this immediately; a system that resists is the most infuriating pattern in support AI.

WHAT A GOOD ESCALATION DOES:
- Says clearly that it is handing off, and to what.
- CARRIES THE CONTEXT. The user should not have to re-explain. Passing a transcript, a summary, and the attempted resolutions is the whole value of the handoff.
- Sets an expectation for time.
- Leaves the user somewhere useful in the meantime, rather than on a dead screen.
- Does not lose the work already done.

ANTI-PATTERNS:
- The deflection loop. The system routes to an FAQ, then back to itself, then to a form. Users experience this as being refused help by a machine designed to prevent them from getting it — and it is the reason support AI has the reputation it has.
- Escalation that drops context, so the human starts from zero and the user repeats themselves.
- Hiding the human option behind repeated failed attempts.
- Escalating everything, which makes the system pointless.

IN AGENTIC SYSTEMS: the same logic governs agent-to-agent and agent-to-human handoffs. See module 47 for handoff protocols.

title: Bias in AI Interfaces — What Design Can Actually Address
content:
Model bias is a model problem. Its expression in the interface is a design problem, and there is more design leverage than usually assumed.

WHERE BIAS BECOMES A DESIGN ISSUE:
- DEFAULTS AND EXAMPLES. The example prompts, sample data, placeholder names, and default avatars you ship teach users what the system is for and who it is for. A set of examples that all assume one context narrows the product's perceived audience.
- INPUT ASSUMPTIONS. Name fields that reject valid names, address forms that assume one country's structure, gender fields with two options, date formats with one convention. These are ordinary form-design failures that AI products reproduce at scale.
- OUTPUT PRESENTATION. Ranked lists imply the ranking is meaningful. A single answer implies there is one. Where the model is less reliable for some inputs, presenting all outputs with identical confidence formatting is a design decision that hides the disparity.
- FEEDBACK LOOPS. If the interface makes it easier to accept than to correct, the majority behaviour gets reinforced and minority cases degrade further.
- PERFORMANCE DISPARITY MADE INVISIBLE. If the system is measurably worse for non-native speakers or unusual data, and the interface gives no signal, those users experience an unreliable product with no explanation.

WHAT TO DO:
- Audit your examples, defaults, and sample data as a set. Whose context do they assume?
- Test the input fields against genuinely diverse real data, not synthetic variations.
- Where the model is known to be weaker, degrade the confidence language rather than the accuracy claim.
- Make correction at least as easy as acceptance.
- Instrument outcomes by segment where you can, so disparity is measurable rather than anecdotal.

WHAT DESIGN CANNOT FIX: the model's underlying distribution. Do not present interface mitigations as having solved a model problem — that is a form of trust laundering.
